tagline: Keeps records in two different apps in step with each other, both ways.
verdictSummary: Albato's distinguishing feature against a one-way automation tool is two-way sync: change a record in either app and the other follows. That is much harder than it sounds, because it needs change detection on both sides, a mapping between two different ids for the same thing, and a rule for what happens when both change between polls. You can build it correctly for two specific APIs in a weekend. Building it for six hundred, and keeping it working as each one changes, is the business.
coreLoopDIY: Connect two APIs you actually use, map their fields to each other, and keep matching records in step in both directions with every conflict logged and resolvable.
whatYouLose: the connector catalogue — hundreds of apps already integrated
the maintained OAuth applications for each of those services
handling for a provider changing its schema underneath you
durable execution: your sync stops when your server does
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the connectors are the product. Writing the sync engine is a weekend; writing and then maintaining the four hundredth integration is a company.
notes: Two-way sync with explicit conflict handling is the angle, deliberately distinct from the one-way trigger-and-action automation tools already in this catalogue.
prompt:
Build a two-way record synchroniser between exactly two APIs the user chooses. Not a general automation platform.

Connections: two named services, each with its credentials encrypted at rest and a documented OAuth or API-key setup. Treat each as a small adapter module implementing four operations: list records changed since a cursor, read one record, create a record, update a record. Everything else in the system works against that interface, so adding a third service later means writing one adapter.

Mapping: a field map between the two schemas, edited in the interface, with a per-field direction (A to B, B to A, or both) and an optional transform expression. Show a live preview of one real record transformed both ways before the mapping is saved.

Identity: a link table storing the pair of ids for every synced record plus a hash of the last-known value on each side. This table is the heart of the system. A record with no counterpart is created; a record with a counterpart is compared.

Change detection: poll each side using its own change cursor where one exists, and fall back to a modified-since query where it does not. Record the cursor after a successful pass so a restart does not replay.

Conflicts, which is where a naive sync silently destroys data. When both sides changed since the last successful pass, do not guess. Apply the configured strategy per mapping: newest wins, side A wins, side B wins, or hold for review. Under hold-for-review, write both versions and a field-level diff into a conflicts queue and sync nothing for that record until a human chooses. Never silently overwrite the losing side without recording what it contained.

Run log: every pass records what it read, what it wrote, what it skipped and why, and every conflict. Any write must be reproducible from the log. Support replay of a single failed record without re-running the pass.

Safety: a dry-run mode that logs every intended write without performing it, and a hard rate limit per service with exponential backoff. Require a dry run to pass before a mapping can be activated for the first time.

Out of scope: a visual workflow builder, branching or conditional logic, more than two services in one sync, and any hosted multi-tenant deployment.

faq.q: Can I migrate my Albato automations?
faq.a: No. Albato's automations are configuration inside its own platform with no meaningful export, and this build's model is different anyway — a two-way mapping rather than a trigger-and-action chain. You describe the sync again from scratch, which for one pair of apps takes an hour.

faq.q: What happens when both sides change the same field?
faq.a: Whatever you configured, and the prompt insists you configure it explicitly. The default in most homegrown syncs is last-writer-wins, which quietly destroys the other edit. The hold-for-review strategy is slower and is the right default for anything you care about.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: A small VPS with PostgreSQL, five to ten dollars a month. The APIs are usually free at personal volumes. The real cost is that the sync only runs while your server does, and a sync that missed a day has more conflicts to resolve when it comes back.

faq.q: What is the one thing that does not survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Adding the third app. Your sync works beautifully between the two services you wrote adapters for, and the next one is another week. Albato's whole value is that the next one is a dropdown.
